pages.x: In about 390 BC a war band of Gauls came south from the Po valley, routed the Roman army at the Allia River, eleven miles from the city, and sacked Rome. Legend says the sacred geese on the Capitol cackled and woke the defenders in time to beat off a night attack on the citadel.

The Gauls agreed to leave for a ransom in gold. When the Romans complained that the weights were false, the story goes, the Gallic chief, Brennus, threw his sword onto the scales and said, "Woe to the conquered." Romans later told how their hero Camillus arrived just in time to drive the Gauls off.

Rome recovered, built a great new wall, and fought its neighbours one by one. When its Latin allies rose against it, Rome crushed them, and in 338 BC bound each city to itself by a separate treaty. The defeated became allies who sent soldiers to Rome's wars, and some were made Roman citizens.

The Samnites, tough hill peoples of the Apennines, were Rome's hardest enemy. In 321 BC their general, Gavius Pontius, trapped a whole Roman army in a mountain pass, the Caudine Forks, and made every man crawl under a yoke of spears in shame. Rome later broke the peace, and fought on.
To move its armies south, Rome began in 312 BC a great road from the city to Capua, named after the censor who built it, Appius Claudius.
pages.fx: The first of the great Roman roads, which in the end ran some 80,000 kilometres across the empire. Parts of the Appian Way are still walked today.

pages.x: In 295 BC the Samnites joined Gauls, Etruscans and Umbrians in a great alliance against Rome. At Sentinum, it is said, the consul Decius Mus offered his life to the gods of the underworld and rode to his death to win the battle, and the allied army was destroyed. Rome was master of central Italy.

Tarentum, the richest Greek city in Italy, called in King Pyrrhus of Epirus, with a professional army and war elephants. He beat the Romans at Heraclea and Asculum, but lost so many men that, the story goes, he said that one more such victory would ruin him. A costly win is still called a Pyrrhic victory.

Pyrrhus went off to fight Carthage in Sicily, came back, and was checked at Beneventum in 275 BC. He sailed home, Tarentum surrendered, and by 264 BC Rome ruled all of Italy south of the Po. That year it answered a call for help from across the strait in Sicily, and went to war with Carthage.

Rome held Italy not by force alone, but with a web of alliances, colonies and roads, and by sharing its citizenship. Its allies' soldiers made its armies almost impossible to wear down, as Hannibal would find. From Italy, Rome went on to conquer the Mediterranean.
